data.title: Middle East Eye: Morning update
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. According to the statement, the separate incidents occurred after the vessels were attempting to pass through an "unauthorised route".
South Korea's anti-piracy Cheonghae unit will expand its operations into waters nearby the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report by the Yonhap News Agency citing the Korean Defence Ministry. The government is set to submit a motion to parliament to extend the period of the unit's deployment to the region, which is expected to expire at the end of this year.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu other senior officials of a "highly explosive and dangerous reality" in the West Bank amid increasing settler violence. Herzog said that the elections in Israel, the US and the Palestinian Authority - which the latter has since been postponed - alongside the olive harvest season are set to "create a highly explosive and dangerous reality".
The US sanctioned two individuals and another entity accused of aiding Iran in sourcing man-portable air-defense systems (Manpads). The statement said that sanctions "close off more of the channels Tehran uses to try to rebuild its arsenal and raise the risk for third-country brokers and suppliers".
A ballistic missile attack which hit Hayfan in Yemen's Taiz governorate, killed four Yemenis from the same family, including three children, on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that Saudi-led coalition attacks over the past 24 hours have reportedly killed around 20 people across Yemen, including in the provinces of al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Saada, and Taiz.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Shot in class: Gaza's children return to school under Israeli fire
data.author: Maha Hussaini
data.summary:
Shot in class: Gaza's children return to school under Israeli fire
Submitted by
Maha Hussaini
on
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:19
In Gaza’s first formal school year since the genocide, Israeli forces intensify shootings targeting teachers and pupils, alongside air strikes on universities
Palestinian children walk to school past the rubble of destroyed buildings as the academic year begins in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 19 September 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP)
Off
Palestinian teacher Sahar Abushbeika was explaining a science lesson to her third-grade pupils when an Israeli bullet struck her lower back, leaving her bleeding in front of her students.
Within seconds, she collapsed as the children gathered around her, screaming for help.
Abushbeika, who teaches at Dawn of Hope, a makeshift tent school in eastern Khan Younis, southern Gaza, says she was shot by Israeli forces on 30 September.
“It was a normal day. Nothing unusual was happening near the school. I arrived in the morning as usual and began explaining the lesson when I suddenly heard what sounded like a drone, followed by a small explosion,” Abushbeika told Middle East Eye.
“I felt something hit my lower back and realised it was a bullet. The pupils panicked, and I tried to calm them down, but they saw the blood, and I fell to the ground. All I remember is the screams of my students before I found myself in hospital.”
After nearly three years of Israeli attacks that have devastated Gaza’s education system and destroyed or damaged more than 97 percent of schools across the Strip, the Ministry of Education, Unrwa and several independent initiatives have established makeshift tent schools to educate hundreds of thousands of school-age children.
But with classrooms and teachers in short supply, schools have introduced rotating shifts. Many pupils receive only about three hours of lessons a day, three days a week.

- Muna Abusneimah, Palestinian mother

data.title: Middle East Eye: Herzog warns Netanyahu of 'highly explosive and dangerous reality' amid rising settler violence
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Herzog warns Netanyahu of 'highly explosive and dangerous reality' amid rising settler violence
Israeli President Isaac Herzog warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu other senior officials of a "highly explosive and dangerous reality" in the West Bank amid increasing settler violence.
"The IDF commanders, the police officers and the Shin Bet personnel present a worrying picture of limited tools and a shortage of manpower," Herzog wrote in the letter sent to Netanyahu, Defence Minister Israel Katz, the Israeli army chief of staff Eyal Zamir and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara.
Herzog said that the elections in Israel, the US and the Palestinian Authority - the latter has since been postponed - alongside the olive harvest season are set to "create a highly explosive and dangerous reality".
"A severe flare-up on the ground is liable to carry severe and far-reaching consequences, both for Israel’s security and its functioning as a sovereign state, and for Israel’s international standing, Diaspora Jewry, the Israeli economy, and more," the Israeli president further warned.
He added that there is a "moral disgrace and the stain on us" when innocent Palestinians are harmed, and stressed that "there is no room for this lawlessness in a sovereign state".

data.title: Middle East Eye: US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices
Tuesday's midterm elections saw a remarkable wave of firsts that may have been unthinkable if US President Donald Trump had not spurred such backlash across the country.
Among them were victories for four state senators-elect and one US congresswoman who all wear the hijab - a record for the country, and certainly a stunning outcome given the rabid anti-Islam rhetoric and threats that have taken hold since the Trump administration swept to power in January 2025.
These are women whose appearance has been caricatured and insulted by corporate media, Republicans, and trolls online, thus putting a direct target on their backs.
Last week, the Muslim Public Affairs Council (Mpac) expressed concern about the escalation of far-right, anti-Muslim provocateurs in the US, because their actions often result in calls for increased law enforcement presence, and could therefore have ended up dissuading Muslim Americans from voting at all.
But while the turnout demographics are still being assessed, several visibly Muslim, young women have now risen to elected office to take matters into their own hands.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran’s IRGC says two tankers, tugboat were ablaze in Hormuz Strait
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Iran’s IRGC says two tankers, tugboat were ablaze in Hormuz Strait
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the statement, the separate incidents occurred after the vessels were attempting to pass through an "unauthorised route",
One large oil tanker was passing through what the IRGC described as an "illegal southern passageway", hitting a mine and catching fire.
Another supertanker, leaving eastern section of the waterway, was caught in a massive fire. A tugboat that was deployed to extinguish the blaze subsequently burst into flames.
"The US regime, which imposes very heavy insurance costs on American taxpayers and its allies in the region by insisting and inciting vessels to violate and pass through mined passages, would not have suffered these heavy losses and a disgraceful electoral defeat if it had had some foresight, instead of paying these costs by releasing Iran's frozen credits, which are not less than half of these costs that have been made so far," the statement added, referring to the nationwide Democrats' sweep during the midterm elections.
"Attempting to break the law in the Strait of Hormuz will not result in anything other than more financial losses and greater political defeats for the US."

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump's midterm defeat gives the Gulf a chance to escape America's forever wars
data.author: Andreas Krieg
data.summary:
Trump's midterm defeat gives the Gulf a chance to escape America's forever wars
Submitted by
Andreas Krieg
on

Regional leaders must use their influence in Congress to prevent another attack on Iran and negotiate a non-aggression pact with Tehran on their own terms
US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance in the Oval Office on 16 March 2026. Vance said on 4 November that the war on Iran was 'the reason we lost' the midterms (Annabelle Gordon/AFP/File photo)
Off
The US midterm elections were fought over the cost of living, the pundits will say. Look closer and a foreign policy verdict comes into view. Voters passed judgment on Washington's role in the Middle East: on its unconditional backing of Israel, and on Donald Trump's war on Iran. Both lost.
Republicans surrendered both houses of Congress, and several states that had voted red for decades turned blue. Commentators have already noted the irony. Trump set out to change the regime in Tehran. Tehran, by outlasting him, helped change the political order in Washington.
The results also mark a turning point for the Israel lobby and its neoconservative hyperactivism. An endorsement from Aipac, the pro-Israel lobby group, once a prized asset, has become a stain that candidates hurry to wash off. The lobby adapted by moving its money through less visible channels.
It spent millions against candidates who questioned America's unequivocal and open-ended military and financial support for an Israeli government that has thrown the region under the bus. In key races, the money failed to move voters.
Michigan offers the clearest case. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who won the state's Senate seat, ran on American interests. His opponents tried to turn the race into a referendum on Israeli ones.

data.title: Middle East Eye: The Trump era is over. The world should take note
data.author: David Hearst
data.summary:
The Trump era is over. The world should take note
Submitted by
David Hearst
on
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 21:38
If the Netanyahu camp is trembling at where the US appears to be headed, Gulf leaders should be in no less of a panic
An Iranian demonstrator carries a placard depicting US President Donald Trump during a rally in Tehran, on 4 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off
It took nine months, but regime change has finally been achieved.
Nine months after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad director David Barnea put the idea into US President Donald Trump’s head that regime change was possible, it has been achieved.
The only variation on the plan that all three men worked on is that regime change has happened in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, Georgia, Florida, and in Congress - not in Tehran.
The war on Iran is the defining mistake of Trump’s second term as president, and of Netanyahu’s final term of office - but Iran is by no means their sole nemesis.
For the president who knew nothing about Iran, it was more than a bet that went sour. The fact that it was all Netanyahu’s idea makes failure even worse for the leader of an “America First” movement. Iran is a quintessentially “foreign war” that proved the principle on which Trump himself campaigned.
Failure in Iran was different for the prime minister who had the Islamic Republic in his sights for most of his adult life.
It was a classic example of military and intelligence overreach. Netanyahu and Mossad thought they could do to a whole country what they thought they had done to two movements: Hamas and Hezbollah. They totally underestimated the power of the Islamic Republic to resist.
But war on Iran, and the economic disaster it unleashed on both sides of the Gulf and beyond - including record prices at gas stations - are not the real cause of the earthquake that has shaken US politics.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?
Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.
The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.
But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.
Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel detains Palestinian activist without charge
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Israel detains Palestinian activist without charge
Israeli police have detained Abed Abou Shhadeh, a former city council representative of the Palestinian community in Jaffa, a southern suburb of Tel Aviv, Al Jazeera reported on Wednesday.
Palestinian legal group Adalah told Al Jazeera that Israeli police searched Abou Shhadeh’s house and arrested him overnight but have not yet charged him with anything.
The rights group said he is currently being held in a detention centre and is due to appear in an Israeli court later on Wednesday.
“This is not a criminal investigation – it is a campaign to silence Arab journalists and political activists,” Adalah said.
Wafa also reported on Wednesday that a Palestinian man and a foreign solidarity activist were injured on Wednesday evening after being beaten by Israeli settlers in the village of al-Duyuk, west of Jericho.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society told Wafa its crews treated the wounded and transferred them both to hospital.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Egyptian doctor who undertook medical missions to Gaza will now go to US Congress
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Egyptian doctor who undertook medical missions to Gaza will now go to US Congress
Egyptian-American surgeon Adam Hamawy has won his bid for Congress in New Jersey’s 12th congressional district, joining the blue wave across the US and making history as the first Muslim and Egyptian American to represent the state.
During his victory speech in the midterm elections on Tuesday, he spoke directly to the people in Gaza, saying: “To the men, women and children of Gaza and Palestine. Your smiles give me the courage and the hope to fight for a better world."
Republicans previously held the majority of the House of Representatives with 218 seats, four more than the Democrats at 215, but come January, Hamawy is one of the congressional wins to give his party a majority. with a whopping projected 250 seats, according to MS Now.
Middle East Eye attended Hamawy's watch party in Princeton, New Jersey, where he declared during his speech that he was ready to get to work and vowed to “hold Donald Trump accountable”.
“I'm a surgeon, and I can tell you that we are going to stop the bleeding. We are going to fight for every American that's been left behind by the establishment that has been ruling Washington for so long.”

data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a Houthi-fired missile in the Medina region
The Saudi-led military coalition said on Thursday it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards the Medina region.
“Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile fired by the Houthi terrorist militia in the Medina region,” the coalition spokesman Colonel Turki Al-Malki said.
Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defence issued an alert for the Yanbu Governorate near the Red Sea in Medina province.
